claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 was previously synthesized with a hierarchical heterostructure exhibiting multilevel chemical fluctuations.

A reduced-order physics-informed ML workflow using a few first-principles descriptors and sparse experimental data can accurately predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness for hierarchical-heterostructured HfNbTiVAl10.
Elastic constants, misfit volumes, unstable stacking-fault energies, and surface energies are physically relevant inputs for models of alloy strengthening and ductility.
The required elastic, misfit-volume, surface-energy, and unstable-stacking-fault descriptors are accessible through first-principles simulations.
A limited set of tensile and fracture-test data is sufficient to train the proposed model for all three target properties.
Multilevel chemical fluctuations and the heterostructured architecture mediate local stress distributions.
Multilevel chemical fluctuations and the heterostructured architecture alter crack-propagation paths.
The heterostructure links atomic-scale descriptors to bulk stiffness, plastic yield, and fracture behavior.
Focusing on physically interpretable local-bonding and defect-energetics descriptors can replace complete CALPHAD and high-throughput DFT analyses for the target predictions.
ML can predict mechanical properties of both single-phase and multiphase alloys with reasonable accuracy.
Existing DFT implementations generally cannot explicitly evaluate fracture or yield strength in alloys.
First-principles simulations remain challenging for disordered multi-principal-element alloys.
Existing strategies require extensive CALPHAD, full-scale first-principles simulations, or brute-force ML on large datasets.
The proposed workflow will reduce computational demands by roughly 50% relative to full-scale CALPHAD and high-throughput DFT.
The proposed workflow will increase yield-strength and Young’s-modulus prediction accuracy from about 90% to about 95%.
The proposed workflow will provide a quantitative estimate of fracture toughness for the first time.
The model is reliable only while the hierarchical heterostructure, local chemical fluctuations, and phase state are preserved.
Annealing, quenching, or testing temperatures that alter phase distribution or induce unmodeled transformations will diminish predictive reliability.
Elevated-temperature strength prediction by ML has been demonstrated for MoNbTaTiW and HfMoNbTaTiZr, although such studies are rare.

A blinded benchmark of at least 20 samples will falsify the hypothesis if measured Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness deviate by more than ±10% from predictions or if trends are missed under structure-preserving modified conditions.
